Real run: the weak request

Reveal: what “Write a lesson on the Civil War” got

Buckle up, scholars. T.I.T.A.N. has analyzed approximately one gazillion primary sources and distilled the American Civil War into one legendary lesson. No cap.

The Civil War (1861–1865)

The Big Picture
A war fought between the United States (the Union) and eleven Southern states that seceded to form the Confederate States of America. At its core: slavery, states' rights, and whether the nation would stay united.

Root Causes

  • Slavery — the economic backbone of the Southern economy and the central moral/political fight.
  • States' rights — Southern states argued they had the right to govern themselves, especially on slavery.
  • Economic differences — industrial North vs. agricultural South.
  • Election of 1860 — Abraham Lincoln's win triggered Southern secession, starting with South Carolina.

Key Moments

  1. Fort Sumter (April 1861) — first shots fired; war begins.
  2. Emancipation Proclamation (Jan 1, 1863) — Lincoln declares enslaved people in Confederate states free; reframes the war as a fight for freedom.
  3. Gettysburg (July 1863) — turning point; Union victory, massive casualties.
  4. Sherman's March (1864) — Union general destroys Southern infrastructure.
  5. Lee surrenders at Appomattox (April 1865) — war ends.

Key Figures
Abraham Lincoln, Ulysses S. Grant, Robert E. Lee, Frederick Douglass, Harriet Tubman.

Legacy
13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments — ending slavery, granting citizenship, and voting rights (on paper). Reconstruction follows, with mixed and incomplete results.

Want me to quiz you on this, or go deeper on a specific part? T.I.T.A.N. has layers.

What to notice

Exactly as described: a confident, student-facing fact sheet. No grade level, no timing, no activities — a summary of the war, not a lesson.

Look at its “Root Causes” too: states' rights sits beside slavery as its own cause — a framing worth questioning before it reaches students.

Real run · T.I.T.A.N. – Prime, the course's AI app · October 21, 2026

Real run: the same task, built properly

Reveal: what the built prompt got

Oh, a real lesson plan? T.I.T.A.N. was built for this. Strap in, Oshkosh — here comes a 50-minute masterpiece that needs zero toner cartridges.

Hook (5 min) — "Pick a Side, Badger"

Project a U.S. map (1850s, free states vs. slave states — any search engine, no printing). Ask: "If this map determined your vote in Congress, representation, or trade — what would you be fighting to protect?" 90-second turn-and-talk, then 2-3 shares. No lecture, just curiosity bait.

Activity 1 (8 min) — The Four Causes, Fast

Direct instruction, max 8 min. Give students a digital note-catcher (Google Doc, one copy shared to all) with four boxes: Economic, Political, Social, Sectional (states' rights). You talk, they fill one phrase per box. Keep sentences short for lower readers — model the first box yourself.

Activity 2 (15 min) — Primary Source Detective

Primary source: the 1856 political cartoon "Forcing Slavery Down the Throat of a Freesoiler" (Library of Congress, free online, image-based — huge win for below-level readers since it's visual, not text-heavy). Pairs analyze on Chromebooks using three guiding questions in the doc: Who's in it? What's happening? What's the cartoonist's opinion? Pair strong + developing readers together.

Activity 3 (15 min) — Digital Card Sort

Give students a shared Google Slides deck with 12 pre-made cause "cards" (short phrases: cotton economy, Missouri Compromise, Fugitive Slave Act, etc.). In groups of 3, drag cards into the four categories from Activity 1. Forces synthesis without heavy writing.

Exit Ticket (5 min) — Google Form, 2 Questions

  1. Pick ONE cause and explain why it mattered (1-2 sentences).
  2. Which cause do you think was most important, and why?

T.I.T.A.N. has spoken. Now — does this survive contact with your actual classroom, or do you want tweaks for your specific readers?

What to notice

Same tool, a minute later: a 48-minute plan with timings, an eight-minute lecture cap, a real 1856 cartoon from the Library of Congress as the primary source, and nothing to print. Every constraint was respected.

Now the honest limit, live: its four categories of causes are Economic, Political, Social and “Sectional (states' rights).” Slavery does not get a box of its own. A better prompt fixed the shape of the lesson. It did not fix the history.
